    __tablename__ = "api_keys"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    vendor_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("vendors.id"), index=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(120))
    prefix: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(20), unique=True, index=True)
    key_hash: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(128), unique=True)
    active: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(Boolean, default=True)
    created_by_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))
    last_used_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(DateTime, nullable=True)
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(DateTime, default=utcnow)
metadata.proof: The APIKey SQLAlchemy model has no `expires_at` column. API keys created via POST /api/vendor/api-keys persist forever with only a boolean `active` flag for revocation. There is no automatic expiry, no rotation policy, and no mechanism to force key renewal. A compromised or leaked API key grants perpetual access to the /api/integrations/order-status endpoint to mutate orders until manually revoked. Contrast with SessionToken which does have expires_at.

extra.message: API Keys Remain Active After Vendor Suspension or User Disablement

metadata.proof: Untrusted source: a previously-issued vendor API key presented as a Bearer token. Sink: the integration order-status endpoint lookup that only checks APIKey.active. Even if the vendor is suspended (Vendor.status != active) or the creating user is disabled, the bearer token is still accepted and can mutate order status for that vendor, because the query never joins Vendor.status or User.disabled.

metadata.proof: Sensitive financial/PII data (tax ID last-4 digits and payout account holder name) are persisted as cleartext database columns in the Vendor model without encryption, hashing, or column-level encryption, exposing the data to anyone with database access or backups.

metadata.proof: GET /api/vendor/products builds a query scoped to the vendor but never applies a LIMIT before calling .all(). A vendor with a large catalog causes the endpoint to load every product row, related vendor/category rows, and serialize them all into a single JSON response, exhausting server memory.

extra.message: Unbounded Vendor Inventory Export Buffering

metadata.proof: GET /api/vendor/exports/inventory.csv materializes every product belonging to the vendor into a Python list and then passes the list to csv_response, which buffers the entire CSV in an io.StringIO object. There is no row limit, so a large vendor catalog can consume unbounded memory during export.
